title: When {recipient} asks again
notes: Lessons talk about one person, so every subject uses {recipient}, never {pronoun}. If Q1 is 'both', use the singular labels for lessons: recipient 'your parent', Recipient 'Your parent', possessive 'your parent's', object 'them'. For 'in_law' and 'other', use the quiz labels.

Variants (set on screen 1) change examples and tasks only. Every variant ends in the same place: the same pattern learned, one saved phrase, one if-then plan. The next lesson never depends on the variant.
'both' uses the in_person texts plus the phone tip on the 'aha' screen.
Every screen shows the line from common.notMedicalAdvice in the footer.

steps.label: Reassure
steps.example: We have plenty of time. I'll tell you when it's time.

steps.label: Offer something to do
steps.example: Want to help me with the tea?

screens.speaker: rosa
screens.text: Let's start with the moment that comes up most.
screens.question: Where do {possessive} repeated questions usually reach you?

in_person.setup: It's 6 pm. {Possessive} doctor appointment is tomorrow. For the fifth time today, {recipient} asks:
in_person.line: When are we going to the doctor?

phone.setup: You're at work. {Recipient} calls for the third time today:
phone.line: When are you coming on Saturday?

not_yet.intro: Many families notice this first. Here's what it often looks like.
not_yet.setup: It's 6 pm. {Possessive} doctor appointment is tomorrow. For the fifth time today, {recipient} asks:
not_yet.line: When are we going to the doctor?

screens.question: What would you say?

in_person.text: It's tomorrow at 2. I wrote it on the calendar for you.
in_person.feedback: Kind and practical. But it answers the fact, not the worry, so the question may come back soon.

in_person.text: Don't worry, I've got it all handled.
in_person.feedback: Reassuring. But "don't worry" can brush the feeling aside, and the worry is still there.

in_person.text: {Recipient}, I told you already. It's tomorrow.
in_person.feedback: Almost everyone says this. You're tired, and it's true. But it reminds {object} of forgetting, which can feel embarrassing, and the worry stays.

in_person.text: You're wondering about tomorrow. We have plenty of time. I'll tell you when it's time. Want to help me with the tea?
in_person.feedback: This names the feeling, reassures {object}, and gives {object} something to do. That's the pattern we'll practice.

phone.text: Saturday morning, around ten. Write it down so you remember.
phone.feedback: Clear and practical. But it answers the fact, not the feeling behind the call, so {recipient} may call again soon.
Warm. But "don't worry" can brush the feeling aside.

phone.text: {Recipient}, I told you already. Saturday. I'm at work.
phone.feedback: Almost everyone says this, especially in the middle of a workday. But it reminds {object} of forgetting, and {recipient} may feel like a bother.

phone.text: You're wondering when I'll come. I'll call you before I leave, so you don't have to keep track. What are you doing right now?
phone.feedback: This names the feeling, takes the job of remembering off {object}, and moves the talk to something new.

screens.afterChoice: You can try another answer to compare.

screens.title: Each time feels like the first time to {object}.
screens.body: {Recipient} isn't testing you, and isn't doing it on purpose. The memory of asking fades, but the feeling behind the question stays. To {object}, the question really is new.

miniTask.question: What might be behind the question?

options.label: Worry
options.response: Often, yes. A plan that feels uncertain can keep coming back as a question.

options.label: Boredom
options.response: It can be. When there's nothing to do, the same thought can loop. Having something to do helps.

options.label: Doing it on purpose
options.response: It can feel that way, especially the fifth time. But {recipient} truly doesn't remember asking. That's why the answer that works is about the feeling, not the facts.

screens.title: Answer the feeling first. Keep it short and the same.
screens.body: Use the three steps: notice the feeling, reassure, offer something to do. Then say it the same short way each time. Long explanations are harder for {object} to follow and tiring for you.

miniTask.question: Which reply follows all three steps?

options.label: It's at 2, like I said. The doctor just wants to check on you, nothing to worry about, and then we'll go home.
options.response: Kind, but long, and it skips the feeling.

options.label: You're wondering about it. I've got it covered. Want to fold these towels with me?
options.response: Yes: feeling, reassurance, something to do.

screens.title: Make the answer easy to find, and don't announce plans too early.

in_person: Put the answer where {recipient} can see it: a note or whiteboard, like "Doctor: Thursday 2 pm. I'll pick you up."
Mention plans closer to the time. A plan announced days ahead gives the worry more time to grow.
phone: Ask {object} to keep a note by the phone with the next visit: "Saturday. I'll call before I leave."
Mention plans closer to the time. A visit announced days ahead gives the worry more time to grow.
not_yet: If it starts, a note or whiteboard with the answer helps: "Doctor: Thursday 2 pm. I'll pick you up."
Mention plans closer to the time. A plan announced days ahead gives worry more time to grow.

screens.extraForBoth: On the phone, a note by the phone works the same way.
screens.extraForFacility: If {recipient} lives in a care home, ask the staff to keep your visit days on a calendar in {possessive} room.
screens.patternTip: Look for a pattern: does it happen at a certain time of day, or after something specific?

screens.title: The fifth time is the hardest.
screens.body: Feeling frustrated is normal. It doesn't make you a bad daughter or son. What helps is a small reset before you answer.

miniTask.question: Pick your reset for next time:

options.label: One slow breath before I answer
Step away for a minute, if it's safe

fallbackScenarios.setup: Ten minutes later, {recipient} asks again, a little more worried:

answers.text: No, nothing's wrong. I already said it's just a checkup.
answers.feedback: True, but "already said" points at the forgetting.

answers.text: You sound worried. I'm right here, and everything's taken care of. Come sit with me?

answers.feedback: It can feel like blame, and {recipient} may not know why either.

fallbackScenarios.line: Why won't you just tell me? You're hiding something.

answers.text: I'm not hiding anything. I've told you five times.
answers.feedback: Defending yourself is natural, but it turns into an argument.

answers.text: It sounds like you feel left out. I'll tell you everything as it happens. Want to look at the calendar together?
answers.feedback: You named the feeling and gave a calm, shared next step.
It answers the question, but not the feeling of being left out.

default.question: Did {recipient} ask the same question again since yesterday?

options.label: Not yet
options.response: Your plan is ready for when it does.

options.label: It helped
options.response: That's real progress. The three steps get easier every time you use them.

options.label: Partly
options.response: That's normal at first. Keep the same words for a few days. Familiar words help.

options.label: It didn't help
options.response: That happens. Here are a few more ways to try.

not_yet.question: Did you notice {recipient} asking the same question again?

options.label: Yes, I noted it
options.response: Thank you. Your notes are on the doctor-visit sheet.

options.label: No
options.response: Good to know. Keep an eye out on your next call or visit.

options.label: Not sure
options.response: That's okay. Small changes are easy to miss. Keep your notes handy.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Look for a pattern
followUpsDidntHelp.text: Does it happen at a certain time of day, when {recipient} is tired, hungry or has nothing to do? Answering that need can help more than any words.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Shorter, and written down
followUpsDidntHelp.text: Use fewer words, the same each time, and point to the note: "It's on the board. I'll tell you when."

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Give {object} something to do
followUpsDidntHelp.text: Folding towels, sorting photos, helping with dinner. Busy hands quiet a worried loop.

doctorNote.text: If repeated questions are new or suddenly much worse, mention it at the next doctor visit.

in_person.line: What day is it? I feel like I should be somewhere.

phone.stage: {Recipient} calls in the evening. You called this morning.
phone.line: I haven't heard from you all week.
